domain: Installability, web app manifest and app identity

items.title: Ship a complete baseline manifest (the identity block)
items.what: One manifest that every page links to, holding the members every engine reads: id, name, short_name, description, start_url, scope, display, background_color, theme_color, icons, plus lang/dir and categories as metadata.
items.why: The manifest is what turns 'a bookmark to a website' into 'an app': OS-level name and icon, its own window or full screen, a splash screen in the app's colours, a title and status bar in the app's colours, and Chrome's install offer. A missing member is the most common reason an app opens in a browser tab, shows a white flash on launch, or gets a generic letter icon.
items.how:
<!-- every page, in <head> -->
<link rel="manifest" href="manifest.webmanifest">

// manifest.webmanifest (served as application/manifest+json)
{
  "id": "/myapp/",
  "name": "My App",
  "short_name": "MyApp",
  "description": "One sentence; Chrome shows it in the install dialog.",
  "lang": "en",
  "dir": "ltr",
  "start_url": "./",
  "scope": "./",
  "display": "standalone",
  "background_color": "#161614",
  "theme_color": "#161614",
  "categories": ["social", "productivity"],
  "icons": [
    { "src": "pwa-64x64.png",   "sizes": "64x64",   "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "pwa-192x192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "pwa-512x512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "maskable-icon-512x512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png", "purpose": "maskable" }
  ]
}

// vite-plugin-pwa: put the same object in VitePWA({ manifest: {...} }) and let pwaAssets generate the icons.
items.support: Manifest: Chrome/Edge 39+/79+, Chrome Android 39+, Samsung 4+, Safari iOS 11.3+ (id from 16.4), Safari macOS 17+ (web apps, Sonoma), Firefox Android 79+ (partial). Firefox desktop ignores most members. description: Chromium 88+ (shown in the rich install UI). categories, lang and dir: spec metadata with no documented visible browser behaviour; stores and catalogs read categories.
items.gotchas: Keep short_name to 12 characters or fewer (home-screen labels truncate). Relative URLs in the manifest (start_url, scope, icons, shortcuts) resolve against the manifest URL. id is the exception: it resolves against the origin (see the next item). Give every icon a type so browsers can skip formats they can't decode. If the manifest sits behind cookie auth, add crossorigin="use-credentials" to the link, because the manifest is fetched without credentials by default. A CSP must allow it via manifest-src. Never rename or move the manifest file after launch: Chrome keys updates to it.

items.title: Pin the app's identity with an explicit, path-qualified manifest id
items.what: id is the app's permanent identity. Browsers compute it by resolving the string against the ORIGIN of start_url, not against the manifest's path, and they drop any fragment. Without an id, start_url becomes the identity.
items.why: A stable id lets you change start_url or the manifest location later without users ending up with a duplicate or orphaned app. It also lets two apps on one origin be told apart.
items.support: Chrome/Edge 96+, Chrome Android 96+, Samsung 17+, Safari iOS 16.4+, Safari macOS 17+. Firefox parses it but does nothing with it. Chrome DevTools > Application > Manifest shows the computed App Id.
items.gotchas: './', '/', 'foo' and '../foo' all resolve against the origin. On a shared origin (GitHub Pages project sites at user.github.io/<repo>/), id './' collides with every other app on that origin that uses '/' or './', and the browser treats them as the same app. Use the full path ('/repo/'). Changing an id later creates a NEW app and orphans existing installs. Chrome 149+ desktop offers migrate_from for same-origin id fixes; the explainer says a same-origin migration can be silent, but check that it has shipped before relying on it. Yurt check: vite.config.ts has id './', which resolves to https://<user>.github.io/.

items.title: start_url and scope: launch where the app lives, keep in-app links in the window
items.what: start_url is the URL the icon opens. scope is the set of URLs that count as 'the app'. Both resolve against the manifest URL, so './' works for apps served from a subpath.
items.why: Navigating outside scope brings back browser UI: a URL toolbar on Android and desktop, an in-app Safari sheet on iOS. That is the strongest 'this is a website' tell inside an installed app. A start_url that needs the network makes the app fail at launch when offline.
items.support: All installing engines: Chrome/Edge/Samsung, Safari iOS 11.3+, Safari macOS 17+ (macOS web apps respect scope from Safari 17.2), Firefox Android.
items.gotchas: Set an explicit id before adding analytics parameters to start_url, because without an id a start_url change alters the app's identity. start_url must be inside scope. Precache the start_url document in the service worker. A trailing slash matters: scope '/app' also matches '/apple'. OAuth or payment pages on other origins open in the in-app browser sheet and come back; test the round trip in standalone mode on iOS. Pre-iOS-26 sites without a manifest used the URL of the page being viewed as the start URL.

items.title: display + display_override: always declare a safe display, layer richer modes on top
items.what: display picks the window type (fullscreen > standalone > minimal-ui > browser, with fallback down that chain). display_override is an ordered list tried before display, for modes like window-controls-overlay and tabbed.
items.why: standalone removes the URL bar and tab strip, which is the biggest single change toward feeling native. window-controls-overlay lets a desktop app draw its own title bar, as Slack, VS Code and Teams do.
items.support: display standalone/browser: Chromium, Safari iOS 11.3+, Safari macOS 17+, Firefox Android. fullscreen and minimal-ui: Chromium and Firefox Android only (not Safari). display_override: Chromium 89+ only (Safari and Firefox ignore it and use display). window-controls-overlay: Chrome/Edge 105+, desktop only. tabbed: Chrome 126+ on ChromeOS only.
items.gotchas: Always set display: engines that don't know display_override read only display. On iOS minimal-ui and fullscreen are not supported, so use standalone. Firefox desktop never matches display-mode: standalone; from Firefox 142, Windows taskbar web apps match minimal-ui. A user's 'open in tab or window' choice on desktop overrides the manifest, so switching display after launch doesn't move existing installs into windows.

items.title: Window Controls Overlay: draw your own desktop title bar
items.what: With display_override window-controls-overlay, an installed desktop window gives the title-bar area to your page. Only the min/max/close controls remain, as an overlay. The free area is exposed through CSS env(titlebar-area-*) and navigator.windowControlsOverlay.
items.why: It removes the thick browser-style title bar above a web app, a 30px 'web' tell on desktop. Search, tabs or a channel name can sit in the title row like a native Electron or Win32 app.
items.support: Chrome/Edge 105+ on Windows, macOS, Linux and ChromeOS, installed app windows only. The env(titlebar-area-*) variables exist from Chrome 93. window-drag (the standard name, values move|none) from Chrome/Edge 152; -webkit-app-region and app-region keep working. Not in Safari or Firefox.
items.gotchas: Users can collapse the overlay (a chevron in the title bar), so always use env() fallbacks and listen for geometrychange (debounce it; it fires on every resize). Drag regions swallow clicks: mark every interactive child no-drag. WebView2 152+ enforces inheritance on app-region. Test without installing via DevTools > Application > Manifest > emulate WCO (Edge 121+ and Chrome).

items.title: Installed-window title text: <meta name="application-title">
items.what: A meta tag whose content Chromium shows in an installed app's title bar next to the app name, in place of document.title (which stays tuned for browser tabs).
items.why: Native apps title their window 'App — Document'. Installed PWAs otherwise repeat the tab title, unread counts and all, which reads as a web page.
items.how:
<meta name="application-title" content="#general">

// keep it in sync with the current view
function setAppTitle(text: string) {
  let m = document.querySelector<HTMLMetaElement>('meta[name="application-title"]');
  if (!m) { m = document.createElement('meta'); m.name = 'application-title'; document.head.append(m); }
  m.content = text;
}
items.support: Chrome/Edge 134+ (desktop installed windows; BCD also lists Chrome Android 134, with no visible effect known). Not in Safari or Firefox (harmless there).
items.gotchas: An empty content shows only the app name. Nonstandard (an Edge explainer), so treat it as progressive enhancement and keep document.title meaningful.

items.title: Know each browser's install path and criteria (the 2026 matrix)
items.what: Each browser decides differently whether to offer installation and how. Chromium checks a manifest and an engagement heuristic before promoting the app; Safari has no requirements; Firefox has its own paths.
items.why: If you know which path the user is on, you can show the right Install button or instructions, and you don't promise an install the browser will never offer.
items.support: beforeinstallprompt/appinstalled: Chromium only (Chrome 44+/61+, Edge 79+, Samsung 5+/8+). Safari: zero installability requirements since Safari 26 (iOS/iPadOS), and Add to Dock with no manifest needed since Safari 17 (macOS Sonoma). Firefox Android: menu install/shortcut. Firefox desktop: Windows taskbar web apps since 143.
items.gotchas: Chrome keeps experimenting with these heuristics, so treat them as hints, not guarantees. Test in Chrome DevTools > Application > Manifest. The Firefox Microsoft Store build can't pin web apps. Opening the app on iOS 26 without the 'Open as Web App' toggle creates a plain bookmark (navigator.standalone stays false).

items.title: Custom Install button: capture beforeinstallprompt, prompt on click, react to appinstalled
items.what: Catch Chromium's install offer, suppress its default UI, and fire it from your own button. Also listen for appinstalled, which fires however the app was installed.
items.why: An 'Install' button in your own design, in context (Settings, after a value moment), converts better than the browser's omnibox icon or Android mini-infobar, and it doesn't look like a browser nag.
items.support: Chrome/Edge desktop and Android, Samsung Internet, Opera. Not Safari (any platform) or Firefox; show instructions there.
items.gotchas: Don't await anything before prompt() in the click handler, or user activation is lost and Chrome rejects. A dismissed prompt may not come back for a while, so don't reshow your button until a new beforeinstallprompt arrives. On Android, appinstalled fires when the user accepts, before the WebAPK is actually on the home screen (seconds later). Hide the button in standalone mode, because the event doesn't fire there. Keep the event out of state stores (it's not serialisable); store a boolean.

items.title: Install promotion UX: ask once, at the right moment, with platform-correct wording
items.what: A single non-blocking suggestion, persisted per device, shown only when installing would help. On Chromium it uses the captured prompt; on Safari it shows steps.
items.why: Native apps never ask you to install themselves, and repeated or blocking install nags are a web tell. A well-timed one-off hint plus a permanent entry in Settings gets installs without annoyance.
items.support: Pattern, so universal. The prompt-backed button is Chromium only. The instruction path covers Safari iOS/iPadOS/macOS and Firefox.
items.gotchas: Persist the 'shown' flag in durable app storage, not sessionStorage. Never block a flow or put the hint above primary actions. On iOS, Safari and the home-screen app do NOT share cookies, localStorage or IndexedDB: anything created before installing (account, local identity, drafts) is missing in the installed app. Either suggest installing before local state exists, or provide a hand-off (sign-in link, QR, export/import). Yurt check: its toast fires after onboarding, so on iOS the installed copy starts without that identity. Verify on a current iOS device.

items.title: iOS/iPadOS: detect the platform correctly and explain Add to Home Screen
items.what: Safari has no install API, so on Apple devices you show steps. iPadOS reports a Mac user agent, so it has to be detected through touch points.
items.why: Telling an iPad user to 'use the browser menu', or not telling them anything, loses the install. Accurate, current steps make home-screen install feel built in.
items.support: Add to Home Screen as a standalone web app: iOS 11.3+ with a manifest or meta tag; every site by default from iOS/iPadOS 26. Third-party iOS browsers can add apps from 16.4.
items.gotchas: If 'Add to Home Screen' is missing, it may be hidden under Edit Actions in the share sheet. The home-screen app has isolated storage from Safari, and each added icon gets its own storage. The name and icon are fixed when the icon is added; later manifest changes don't update them. Don't use navigator.platform (deprecated); maxTouchPoints is the stable iPad signal.

items.title: Apple meta tags that still matter (and the Chrome-friendly twin)
items.what: The legacy apple-* meta tags still control the iOS home-screen title, status bar style and splash-screen use. mobile-web-app-capable is the standard twin that keeps Chrome from logging a deprecation warning.
items.why: Without them iOS may label the icon with the page title, keep an opaque status bar that clashes with the app, or skip your startup images. With black-translucent the app paints under the status bar edge to edge, like a native app.
items.how:
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover">
<meta name="mobile-web-app-capable" content="yes">
<meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-capable" content="yes">
<meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-title" content="MyApp">
<meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-status-bar-style" content="black-translucent">

/* content now sits under the status bar: pad the top bar */
.app-header { padding-top: env(safe-area-inset-top); }
items.support: Safari iOS/iPadOS (all current versions). status-bar-style values: default | black | black-translucent. Chrome reads mobile-web-app-capable and warns on apple-mobile-web-app-capable alone.
items.gotchas: From iOS 26, apple-mobile-web-app-capable no longer decides whether the site opens as a web app (every site does by default), but keep it: apple-touch-startup-image splash screens are reported not to show without it. With black-translucent the status bar text is light, so check legibility in light themes and handle the top inset yourself. Don't add maximum-scale or user-scalable=no to stop zoom: it blocks pinch zoom and fails axe.

items.title: apple-touch-icon: one opaque 180x180 PNG
items.what: The home-screen icon on iOS and iPadOS. If it is present, it wins over manifest icons.
items.why: A transparent or missing apple-touch-icon renders as a black tile or a screenshot-like thumbnail. That is the first thing a user sees and an instant tell that it's 'just a website'.
items.how:
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="apple-touch-icon-180x180.png">
<!-- 180x180 PNG, square, NO transparency (flatten onto your brand/background colour), no pre-rounded corners -->
items.support: Safari iOS/iPadOS. Since iOS 15.4 (Safari macOS 17), if there's no apple-touch-icon, manifest icons are used, but only ones with purpose any or no purpose.
items.gotchas: iOS ignores the alpha channel (transparent becomes black) and applies its own corner mask. iOS 18+ dark and tinted home-screen styles are derived automatically, with no per-mode icon member for web apps. Icons don't update after adding; users must remove and re-add. Keep important content inside roughly the central 80%.

items.title: iOS launch (splash) screens with apple-touch-startup-image
items.what: Per-device launch images, matched with exact device-width/height/pixel-ratio/orientation media queries. iOS does not build a splash screen from the manifest.
items.why: Without them an iOS home-screen app launches into a blank screen before first paint. A branded launch image in the page's own colour reads as a native cold start.
items.support: Safari iOS/iPadOS home-screen web apps. Safari 26.0 release notes say nothing new about startup images.
items.gotchas: Each image must match a device exactly; a new iPhone size gets a blank launch until you regenerate (the generators ship device tables, last updated for iPhone 17 / Air). They are reported not to show without apple-mobile-web-app-capable. Dark variants follow the system setting at the time the icon was added and don't react to later changes. Dozens of PNGs: exclude them from service-worker precache. Android builds its splash from the manifest (name, background_color, icon), so it needs nothing extra.

items.title: Generate every icon from one SVG; get maskable right
items.what: Generate one source of truth into the minimum set: favicon.ico (48), an SVG favicon, PNG 64/192/512 with purpose any, a 512 maskable, and a 180 apple-touch-icon. Optionally add a monochrome icon.
items.why: Android masks icons to circles or squircles. A non-maskable icon gets shrunk onto a white disc, which looks foreign next to native apps. Inconsistent hand-made sizes drift apart over time.
items.support: Manifest icons: Chromium, Firefox Android, Safari (fallback only). purpose maskable: Chrome Android (WebAPK adaptive icons) and ChromeOS. purpose monochrome is specified (the alpha channel is used as a mask), but visible use by current browsers is not documented, so treat it as future-proofing.
items.gotchas: Don't declare one file as purpose "any maskable": it gets either too much padding or a clipped logo. Ship separate files. Provide PNGs; SVG manifest icons aren't reliably used for WebAPKs. Preview masks at maskable.app. Desktop Chrome doesn't update installed icons by bitmap comparison; the icon URL has to change (see manifest updates).

items.title: background_color and theme_color = your page surface colour
items.what: background_color fills the launch or splash screen and the window before CSS loads. theme_color tints the Android status bar and task switcher and desktop title bars. Set both to the exact page background.
items.why: Matching colours make launch to first paint seamless (no white flash in a dark app) and make the system bars look like part of the app instead of a browser frame.
items.support: background_color: Chromium 46+, Firefox Android 79+ (Android splash and desktop window). theme_color: Chromium, Firefox Android, Safari iOS 15+, Safari macOS 17+ (web app title bar; fixed in 17.2).
items.gotchas: The manifest can't vary these by colour scheme: the user_preferences.color_scheme proposal is unshipped. Pick the default theme's colour and override theme at runtime with meta theme-color. Android 12+ splash shows the icon in a circle on background_color, so check contrast. Changing the colours after install takes effect only after the browser's next manifest update.

items.title: meta theme-color: per scheme, and kept in sync with an in-app theme switch
items.what: <meta name="theme-color"> overrides the manifest theme_color per page and can be updated at runtime. A media attribute picks a colour per OS scheme.
items.why: System bars that change with the app's light or dark theme (and with modal or overlay states) look native. A dark status bar over a light app looks like a broken website.
items.how:
<meta name="theme-color" content="#ffffff" media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)">
<meta name="theme-color" content="#161614" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)">

// App has its own theme toggle? The media attribute only follows the OS, so collapse to one tag:
export function syncThemeColor() {
  const color = getComputedStyle(document.body).backgroundColor;   // the real page surface
  document.querySelectorAll('meta[name="theme-color"]').forEach((m) => m.remove());
  const meta = Object.assign(document.createElement('meta'), { name: 'theme-color', content: color });
  document.head.append(meta);
}
// call after every theme change
items.support: Chrome 73+ desktop: installed apps only. Chrome Android: browser UI (not with native dark mode unless installed or TWA). media attribute: Safari 15+, Chrome 93+ (installed apps). Safari 26 (iOS and macOS) uses theme-color only for installed web apps; browser tabs tint from the page itself.
items.gotchas: Safari 26 tabs derive the toolbar tint from the body or html background or a position:fixed element at the top. A fixed, coloured header can tint the toolbar unexpectedly, so give the top-most fixed bar the page colour or test. Users can turn tinting off. Firefox ignores theme-color. Yurt check: index.html hard-codes #161614 while store.ts switches data-theme at runtime, so call a sync on theme change.

items.title: Detect 'running as the installed app' robustly (and watch for changes)
items.what: Combine the display-mode media queries with iOS's navigator.standalone, and subscribe to changes. Installs and 'open in app' can move a running page between a tab and a window.
items.why: It drives 'hide Install UI', 'show the in-app back button' and 'pad for the title bar' logic. Getting it wrong shows install nags inside the installed app.
items.support: display-mode: Chrome 42+, Safari 13+, Firefox 47+. Firefox desktop never matches standalone; it matches minimal-ui for Windows taskbar apps from 142. navigator.standalone: Safari iOS/iPadOS only (nonstandard).
items.gotchas: BCD documents a WebKit quirk (bug 264218): in an iOS home-screen app with display standalone, (display-mode: standalone) can be false and (display-mode: fullscreen) true. navigator.standalone is the reliable iOS signal. Only add fullscreen to APP_MODES if your manifest uses it, because Chromium desktop can match it for F11 or the Fullscreen API. 'Installed' isn't knowable from a tab: an installed app can be open in a browser tab. Yurt check: lib/pwa.ts isStandalone tests only display-mode: standalone; add navigator.standalone and minimal-ui/WCO.

items.title: App icon badge (Badging API)
items.what: navigator.setAppBadge(n) and clearAppBadge() put an unread count or a dot on the installed app's icon (Dock, taskbar, home screen). They are also available in the service worker.
items.why: An unread count on the icon is one of the clearest 'this is a real app' signals for chat and mail.
items.support: Chrome/Edge 81+ on Windows and macOS (ChromeOS 91+; Linux shows nothing). Safari macOS 17+ (Sonoma web apps). Safari iOS/iPadOS 16.4+ home-screen apps, only after notification permission is granted. Not Chrome Android: Android shows notification dots instead. Not Firefox.
items.gotchas: Calls reject or no-op outside an installed app; catch and ignore. On iOS ask for notification permission (from a user gesture) or the badge never shows. Declarative Web Push (Safari 18.4+) can set the badge from the payload with app_badge, with no service worker code. Clear the badge when the user reads, not only on launch. TypeScript's lib.dom declares the methods as always present, so use an 'in' check rather than optional chaining.

items.title: Tab-icon and title badges as the fallback when not installed
items.what: Draw the unread count or status onto the favicon with a canvas, and prefix document.title, for users in a browser tab or on browsers without the Badging API.
items.why: Desktop users who never install still get native-feeling 'you have messages' feedback in the tab strip.
items.support: Dynamic favicons: Chromium, Firefox, Safari macOS. iOS Safari doesn't show favicons in tabs.
items.gotchas: Keep the original href and restore it. Safari prefers ICO over PNG when both are declared, so swap the link it actually uses. Don't do this in the installed app when the Badging API exists (it would double-signal). Throttle updates.

items.title: Richer install dialog: description + screenshots with form_factor
items.what: With description and at least one screenshot for the current form factor, Chromium shows an app-store-style install sheet instead of the small default prompt.
items.why: It looks like a store listing (screenshots, description), so installing feels like getting an app, not bookmarking a page.
items.support: Chrome Android and Chrome/Edge desktop. Desktop shows only form_factor wide screenshots (Chrome 109+). Ignored by Safari and Firefox. Stores and PWABuilder also read screenshots, and the spec has a platform field.
items.gotchas: Constraints: 320-3840px per side; long side ≤ 2.3× short side; identical aspect ratio within a form factor; PNG or JPEG are the documented formats (WebP not guaranteed); up to 8 shown. The description is truncated after about 7 lines (~324 characters). Label every screenshot, since it's the alt text. Exclude screenshots from SW precache.

items.title: App shortcuts (long-press / right-click / Dock menu)
items.what: The shortcuts member adds quick actions to the app icon's context menu: Android long-press, Windows taskbar jump list, macOS Dock and File menu, ChromeOS shelf.
items.why: Long-press actions on the icon are a hallmark of native apps.
items.support: Chrome Android 84+, Chrome/Edge desktop 96+ (Windows-only from 85), Samsung 14+, Safari macOS 17.4+ (Dock and File menu; users can bind keyboard shortcuts in System Settings). Not iOS, not Firefox.
items.gotchas: URLs must be inside scope. The OS may truncate the list (Android launchers show about 4), so put the most important first. Provide 96x96 PNG icons (Android). Shortcut changes reach installed apps only on the next manifest update. Localize names with shortcuts_localized (Chrome 148+).

items.title: Share target: appear in the system share sheet
items.what: share_target registers the installed app as a destination in the OS share sheet. Text and URLs come in by GET; files come in by POST multipart, intercepted in the service worker.
items.why: 'Share to MyApp' from Photos or another app's share menu is deep OS integration that a website can't have.
items.support: Chrome Android 76+, Samsung 12+. BCD lists Chrome/Edge desktop 89+, where OS integration is mainly ChromeOS; verify Windows and macOS. Not Safari (any) or Firefox.
items.gotchas: Only works for installed apps. POST needs the SW, so make sure it's active before the first share; GET with text-only params needs no SW. Treat shared data as untrusted input (schema-validate). Many share sources put the URL in text, not url. Android picks the share label from the app name.

items.title: File handlers + launchQueue: 'Open with MyApp'
items.what: file_handlers registers the installed desktop app for file types at OS level. Opened files arrive through window.launchQueue as FileSystemFileHandles.
items.why: Double-clicking a file in Finder or Explorer and having your app open it is a defining desktop-app behaviour.
items.support: Chrome/Edge 102+ desktop (Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS). Not Android, Safari or Firefox.
items.gotchas: The action must be in scope. The first open asks the user to allow the association. setConsumer must be called on every launch, early. Files arrive on the main thread, not in the SW. With launch_handler focus-existing the files come to the already-open window.

items.title: Protocol handlers: own a web+ scheme (invite links, deep links)
items.what: protocol_handlers in the manifest, or navigator.registerProtocolHandler at runtime, routes links like web+myapp:… (or safelisted schemes such as mailto) to the app.
items.why: Custom-scheme deep links that open the installed app are how native apps take invites and cross-app links.
items.support: Manifest protocol_handlers: Chrome/Edge 96+ desktop. registerProtocolHandler: Chrome 13+, Edge 79+, Firefox 2+ (desktop and Android). Not Safari.
items.gotchas: Custom schemes need the web+ prefix plus lowercase letters, unless safelisted (mailto, magnet, matrix, …). The browser asks the user on first use. The handler receives untrusted input. Plain https links into your scope are usually better: navigation capturing and launch_handler handle those.

items.title: Single-instance launches: launch_handler + launchQueue (and Chrome's link capturing)
items.what: launch_handler.client_mode controls whether launches (icon, shortcut, captured link, file) open a new window or reuse an existing one: focus-existing, navigate-existing, navigate-new or auto. The target URL arrives through launchQueue.
items.why: Native chat or mail apps have one window. Clicking a link should focus it and route in place, not spawn a second copy that reloads, reconnects and loses state.
items.support: launch_handler: Chrome/Edge 110+ (desktop and Android), Samsung 21+. launchQueue.targetURL: Chrome/Edge 110+. Desktop Chrome 139+ captures clicks on in-scope https links into the installed app by default (Windows, macOS, Linux); ChromeOS from 152. Users can opt out per app. Not Safari or Firefox. Safari macOS Sequoia web apps open in-scope links from other apps.
items.gotchas: focus-existing doesn't navigate: you must consume targetURL or the click looks ignored. Because link capturing is now on by default, test what happens when a user clicks your link in email or chat with the app installed. handle_links ("preferred") remains an incubation; launch_handler is the shipped control.

items.title: scope_extensions: one app across several origins
items.what: Extends the app's scope to other origins, which must opt in via /.well-known/web-app-origin-association. Navigations there stay in the app window.
items.why: Without it, moving from app.example.com to auth.example.com or a locale domain pops browser UI inside the installed app.
items.support: Chrome/Edge 138+ (desktop and Android), Samsung 30+. Not Safari or Firefox.
items.gotchas: The association keys are the app's resolved id, so a wrong id silently breaks it. Serve the file as JSON over HTTPS at the origin root (impossible on a shared host such as a GitHub Pages project site). The same file carries allow_migration for origin migrations.

items.title: Localized app name, description, icons and shortcuts (*_localized)
items.what: name_localized, short_name_localized, description_localized, icons_localized and shortcuts_localized map BCP 47 tags to values. The browser picks the best match for the user's language.
items.why: A home-screen or Start-menu label in the user's language matches what native apps do.
items.support: Chrome/Edge 148+ desktop (BCD manifests.webapp.localized_members). Not Chrome Android, Safari or Firefox. They fall back to the base members.
items.gotchas: More specific tags win (fr-CA falls back to fr). Values can be strings or {value, lang, dir} objects. Keep base members in your default language.

items.title: related_applications, prefer_related_applications, getInstalledRelatedApps
items.what: Declares your native or store apps, or the PWA itself. Lets a page ask whether one is installed, and can make Chromium Android offer the store app instead of the PWA.
items.why: Lets you hide 'Install' or 'Get the app' when the user already has it, and switch to an 'Open app' affordance like native smart banners.
items.support: getInstalledRelatedApps: Chrome Android 84+ (PWA and Android-app checks, Android apps via Digital Asset Links), Chrome/Edge desktop 85+ on Windows for UWP apps only (empty array elsewhere). related_applications/prefer: Chrome Android, Edge, Samsung. Not Safari (use Apple Smart App Banners for App Store apps) or Firefox.
items.gotchas: prefer_related_applications: true makes the PWA uninstallable in Chromium. Self-detection of the PWA works best on Android; don't build desktop logic on it.

items.title: Plan for manifest updates and identity changes
items.what: Installed apps update from the manifest on the browser's own schedule. Name and icon changes need user confirmation. iOS never updates a home-screen icon. Chrome 149+ desktop can migrate an installed app to a new id or origin.
items.why: Native apps update cleanly. A web app stuck with an old icon, a duplicate install after a URL change, or a surprise 'App update available' dialog all feel broken.
items.support: Chrome desktop: from Chrome 144, update checks are reportedly cheaper and deterministic; name and icon changes show a 'Review app update' prompt. Chrome Android (WebAPK): checks on launch, re-mints the WebAPK and asks for confirmation on significant icon/name changes. iOS/iPadOS: name and icon are frozen at Add to Home Screen. migrate_from/migrate_to: Chrome/Edge 149+ desktop (BCD). Chrome's blog says 150.
items.gotchas: If the manifest 404s, Chrome may stop checking for about 30 days. Display-mode changes don't override a user's tab-or-window choice. Origin migrations don't carry permissions (notifications must be re-granted). A forced migration applies only the URL change, and name or icon changes are deferred. Test with chrome://web-app-internals.

items.title: Orientation: usually omit it; know what 'any' does
items.what: orientation sets the default orientation of the installed app. On Android it becomes the activity's requested orientation; iOS and desktop ignore it.
items.why: Locking a phone app to portrait matches many native apps. But a lock that fights the user's rotation setting, or flips upside down, feels broken.
items.support: Manifest orientation: Chrome Android 39+, Firefox Android 79+, Samsung 4+. Ignored by Safari iOS and desktop browsers. Android 16 (API 36) ignores orientation locks on screens ≥600dp (tablets, foldables) for apps targeting 36. ScreenOrientation.lock: Chrome Android, Firefox 144+; desktop Chrome always throws.
items.gotchas: In current Chromium, 'any' maps to SCREEN_ORIENTATION_FULL_USER: it respects the rotation lock but allows 180° upside-down portrait on phones. Older Chrome versions mapped 'any' to full-sensor, which ignored the user's rotation lock. Design layouts for both orientations on tablets regardless. Yurt check: the manifest sets orientation 'any'; consider omitting it.

items.title: macOS Safari 'Add to Dock' web apps: what they inherit
items.what: Safari 17+ (macOS Sonoma and later) turns any site into a Dock app via File > Add to Dock, using the manifest when present.
items.why: Mac users get a real app: its own window, Dock icon, Cmd-Tab entry, notifications and badges. Knowing its rules avoids broken logins and odd title bars.
items.support: Safari 17+ macOS Sonoma, Sequoia, Tahoe. Badging and Web Push work in Dock apps. Since macOS Sequoia (Safari 18), in-scope links clicked in other apps open in the web app. Safari 26 drops the manifest requirement entirely.
items.gotchas: At creation Safari copies the site's cookies into the app (the user stays signed in) but not localStorage or IndexedDB, and nothing is shared afterwards. Apps that keep identity client-side (IndexedDB) start empty, the same as on iOS. Scope defaults to the host when there's no manifest. minimal-ui and fullscreen aren't supported (BCD), so use standalone.

items.title: Google Play via Trusted Web Activity (Bubblewrap / PWABuilder)
items.what: Wrap the PWA in a tiny Android app that renders it full screen in Chrome (a TWA). Digital Asset Links verify that you own the origin.
items.why: Store discovery, store reviews and installs survive device restore, and to the user it's an Android app with no browser UI.
items.how:
npx @bubblewrap/cli init --manifest https://example.com/app/manifest.webmanifest
npx @bubblewrap/cli build      # -> app-release-bundle.aab (+ signed APK)

// https://example.com/.well-known/assetlinks.json   (origin ROOT, not /app/)
[{ "relation": ["delegate_permission/common.handle_all_urls"],
   "target": { "namespace": "android_app", "package_name": "com.example.app",
               "sha256_cert_fingerprints": ["<Play App Signing key SHA-256 from Play Console>"] } }]
items.support: Android with a TWA-capable browser (Chrome, and others with Custom Tabs support). @bubblewrap/cli 1.25 (Sept 2026). PWABuilder generates the same, plus Windows and iOS packages.
items.gotchas: With Play App Signing, use the Play-managed key's fingerprint, not your upload key, or the URL bar appears. assetlinks.json must be at the origin root, so a GitHub Pages project site (user.github.io/repo) can't host it unless you control user.github.io or use a custom domain. Digital goods must follow Play billing policy. App Store wrappers (WKWebView) risk rejection under minimum-functionality rules.

items.title: Microsoft Store via PWABuilder (MSIX), plus Edge-only extras
items.what: Package the PWA as an MSIX with PWABuilder and submit it in Partner Center. No code changes.
items.why: The app shows up in the Windows Store and Start-menu search like any Windows app. Store installs also get automatic link handling.
items.support: Windows 10/11. Individual developer accounts have been free since 2025; secondary sources report company accounts free from May 2026.
items.gotchas: Store-installed PWAs capture in-scope links automatically (users can opt out in edge://apps). Edge's 'widgets' manifest member (Windows 11 Widgets Board, Adaptive Cards) is niche. edge_side_panel (Edge sidebar) is being deprecated as of July 2026, so don't adopt it.

items.title: Upcoming: navigator.install() and the <install> element
items.what: A standard, user-activated way to start installation of the current app (or another app by manifest URL) without beforeinstallprompt, plus a declarative, browser-rendered <install> button.
items.why: It will replace the event-capture dance with a reliable Install button that works whenever the browser can install.
items.support: Experimental. Web Install API origin trial in Chrome/Edge 143–148 (extended to 150), with an intent to ship on desktop around M156; Android later. BCD: navigator.install and <install> in Chrome/Edge 154 behind #web-app-installation-api. The <install> origin trial ran 148–153 with older attribute names (installurl/manifestid); the current explainer uses manifest/manifestId. Mozilla and WebKit positions are pending.
items.gotchas: The API shape has changed during trials; don't ship without feature detection and a beforeinstallprompt/instructions fallback. Errors: NotAllowedError (no user activation), DataError (bad manifest or id mismatch), AbortError (user cancel). Permissions-Policy web-app-installation gates cross-origin use.

items.title: Type and feature-detect the non-standard install APIs
items.what: TypeScript's lib.dom (5.9) has setAppBadge/clearAppBadge but none of beforeinstallprompt, navigator.standalone, windowControlsOverlay, launchQueue or getInstalledRelatedApps. Declare them as optional so every call site has to feature-detect.
items.why: It removes casts and the 'works on Chrome, crashes on Safari' class of bugs that make an app feel flaky.
items.support: Not applicable (typing only). Matches BCD support for each API.
items.gotchas: Don't declare beforeinstallprompt in WindowEventMap as BeforeInstallPromptEvent: it would claim the type on Safari and Firefox too. Narrow it at runtime. Results of getInstalledRelatedApps and launch params are external input: validate them.

items.title: Niche or legacy manifest members: what to skip
items.what: A map of members you'll see in generators and docs that are platform-locked, deprecated or nonstandard.
items.why: It avoids cargo-culting dead members that bloat the manifest or imply features users will never see.
items.support: As listed (BCD 8.1.4, Edge docs July 2026).
items.gotchas: Unknown members are ignored, not errors, so the risk is wasted effort and false expectations rather than breakage.
